title: Physics-aware initialized 22-layer ZnS/MgF2 defect-cavity dual-band IR filter
scientific_hypothesis: Initializing layer thicknesses around calculated quarter-wave (Bragg mirror) and half-wave (defect cavity) values with ±5% perturbation will achieve higher best_target_score and maintain tightest_margin compared to uniform or random initialization, because the search begins within the resonant optical path length basin.
design_principle: Distributed Bragg reflectors (alternating high/low index quarter-wave layers) create high-reflectance stopbands. A central defect cavity (half-wave optical thickness) breaks the periodicity and creates transmission peaks within the stopband. For dual-band transmission, the defect region thickness and surrounding mirror symmetry determine peak positions and widths.
design_variables: individual layer thicknesses for all 22 layers, initialized around physics-calculated quarter-wave and half-wave values with ±5% Gaussian perturbation
soft_objectives: maximize mean transmittance in 4.15-4.35 μm band
maximize mean transmittance in 4.55-4.75 μm band
minimize mean transmittance in 3.60-4.00 μm band
minimize mean transmittance in 4.85-5.20 μm band
manufacturing_considerations: layer thicknesses should remain within depositable ranges 50-1000 nm
theory_basis: Quarter-wave optical thickness (t = λ/4n) creates maximum reflectance for Bragg mirrors at design wavelength
Half-wave optical thickness (t = λ/2n) in defect cavity creates transmission resonance within Bragg stopband
Symmetric mirror structures around defect cavity improve peak transmission and reduce sideband ripple
ZnS (high index ~2.3) and MgF2 (low index ~1.35) provide sufficient index contrast for mid-IR Bragg mirrors
Dual transmission peaks can be achieved by tuning defect cavity thickness to support multiple resonant modes
expected_advantages: Faster convergence due to physics-aware initialization
Higher best_target_score compared to uniform 100nm starting point
Better preservation of tightest_margin across optimization rounds
known_risks: Refractive index values for ZnS and MgF2 at 4-5 μm are recalled approximations (ZnS ~2.2-2.4, MgF2 ~1.3-1.4); exact dispersion data from registry will determine actual quarter-wave thicknesses
Dual-band transmission with single defect cavity may not achieve both passbands equally; may require asymmetric mirror design or multiple defects
22 layers may not provide sufficient stopband rejection; 24 layers could improve but was not chosen to maintain comparability with prior iteration
Quarter-wave calculation uses single center wavelength (~4.4 μm) but passbands span 4.15-4.75 μm; broadband performance may differ from narrowband design
Daimon-20 substrate dispersion in mid-IR range is recalled but not verified against registry data
execution_request_english: Optimize a 22-layer multilayer infrared filter on CaF2 (Daimon-20) substrate with air incidence at normal angle. Stack sequence: zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2/zns/mgf2 (22 layers total, alternating). Initialize layer thicknesses using physics-aware bootstrap: calculate quarter-wave thickness t = λ_center/(4×n) for Bragg mirror layers using λ_center = 4400 nm and estimated effective indices (zns n≈2.3, mgf2 n≈1.35), calculate half-wave thickness t = λ_center/(2×n) for central defect cavity layers (layers 11-12), then apply ±5% Gaussian perturbation to create initial population. Optimize all 22 individual layer thicknesses to maximize mean transmittance in passbands 4150-4350 nm and 4550-4750 nm while minimizing mean transmittance in stopbands 3600-4000 nm and 4850-5200 nm. Use coherent thin-film matrix method. Spectral evaluation range 3500-5300 nm. No metal layers. Maximum layer thickness 1000 nm, minimum 50 nm.
revision_reason: Repair material name ambiguity: replaced CaF2 with Daimon-20 substrate per registry resolution requirement. CaF2 matched 4 datasets equally; Daimon-20 is one of the two accepted diagnostic names that pins exactly one dataset.
